analysis.one_liner: Ordered US troops and defense contractors out of Iraq by mid-2008.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, it got no hearing and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Defense Secretary to start pulling US troops and Defense Department-funded contractors out of Iraq within 90 days and finish by June 30, 2008. It allowed small forces to stay for embassy security, counterterrorism strikes, and training Iraqi troops, and barred new deployments to Iraq without fresh congressional approval. It also would have handed US-built military bases in Iraq over to the Iraqi government.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families, who would have been redeployed out of the Iraq war; taxpayers, who would stop paying for the occupation; and Iraqis, since US-built bases would transfer to Iraq's government.

how_it_helps.text: Requires redeployment of US forces and Defense Department-funded contractors from Iraq to begin within 90 days and be complete by June 30, 2008 [S2][S3].
Bars further deployments of US forces to Iraq after the redeployment unless Congress specifically authorizes them in advance [S2][S3].
Transfers to the Iraqi government all US right, title, and interest in military facilities built with Defense Department funds and occupied by US forces [S2][S3].
Protects Iraqis endangered by the withdrawal by preserving the President's authority to arrange asylum or other protection for them [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors operating in Iraq on Defense Department funding, whose revenue depended on the US presence, and the defense establishment whose Iraq operations would wind down. Americans who favored continuing the Iraq mission would lose the policy they backed.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges the withdrawal could physically endanger Iraqi citizens who had worked with US forces, which is why it preserves the President's authority to arrange asylum or other protection for them [S2][S3].
It left in place US forces for 'targeted special actions' against al-Qaeda and for training Iraqi troops, so the US military role in Iraq would not have ended entirely [S2][S3].

A hard end date without a negotiated security agreement with Iraq could have created instability on the ground; supporters answered this with a safe-and-orderly redeployment provision and allowances for reconstruction completion, but critics could fairly call the timeline rigid [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill set a firm end to the Iraq deployment with genuine safeguards: limited retention for embassy security and counterterrorism, funding for an orderly withdrawal, transfer of bases to Iraq, and protection for Iraqis at risk. Its main weaknesses were the fixed deadline's rigidity and the fact that a withdrawal of this scale always carries real risks for Iraqis who had sided with the US. The costs fell mostly on contractors and the continuation of an unpopular war, not on ordinary Americans.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: David Obey and James McGovern introduced the bill on May 23, 2007 [S1][S3].
It was referred that same day to the House Armed Services Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 110th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors funded by the Defense Department in Iraq, and officials pursuing the continuation of the Iraq deployment, were better off because the bill never advanced. Troops stayed in Iraq through the end of the Congress and beyond.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Iraq-based contractors and the war's continuation

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; the only two members attached to the bill were Democrats, and the committees that never acted had Democratic chairs.

industries.note: The bill explicitly required contractors funded by the Defense Department to redeploy out of Iraq by June 30, 2008, ending their revenue stream from the occupation [S2][S3]. Their business interest ran directly against the bill's goal of bringing forces home.
Most US-funded Iraq work would end with the withdrawal, though the bill allowed Army Corps of Engineers personnel and reconstruction contractors to stay at Iraq's request to finish projects [S3].
